newsitem.title: USA: Analysts cheer S&P's upgrade of Argentina, Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Analysts cheer S&P's upgrade of Argentina, Brazil.

text.p: Emerging market debt analysts cheered news of the credit rating upgrades on Argentina and Brazil by Standard and Poor's Corp but many believed the upgrades, particularly on Argentina, were long overdue.

"I think the upgrades were long overdue," said Marco Santamaria, vice president of fixed-income research at ING Barings in New York. He said ING's sovereign risk model, which tries to quantify soverign credit risk and link that to sovereign ratings, had both Brazil and Argentina as "clear upgrade candidates."

Though the upgrades of both Argentina and Brazil provided a slight pop in the Brady assets of both countries, market experts were divided over the longer view given the the underlying bearish tone of the U.S. Treasury bond market .

"It might help mitigate some of the trends we are seeing but I don't think it will be able to reverse this overall bear market that we are entering into," said Walter Molano, director of economic and financial research at SBC Warburg.

Thomas Trebat, head of Citicorp Securiites' emerging market research, said: "I think it helps them through a short-term period of Treasury market volatility that lies ahead. I think the impact of Treasury volatility is going to be muted somewhat by these actions and I think it...moves them closer to much larger pools of capital that will only invest in the more highly rated countries."

"I think it is very positive because more conservative investors, who have rating constraints, will be able to have more leeway at looking at those credits," said Joyce Chang, director of emerging market research at Merrill Lynch & Co.
At 1645 EST/2145 GMT, Argentine FRBs were 1/8 stronger at 89-3/4 and Brazilian "C" bonds were 1/4 firmer at 75 bid.

S&P upgraded Argentina's $62.2 billion of long-term foreign currency debt to BB from BB-minus, as well as Brazil's $54.1 billion of long-term foreign currency debt, including the Brady bonds, to BB-minus from B-plus.
Although the credit rating upgrade by S&P was welcomed by the market, sources said an upgrade by Moody's Investors Service Inc would help to boost prices further.
"If Moody's were to upgrade both Brazil and Argentina, then surely that would provide further impetus and you get a much bigger response to the market than you did just now."
As for the long-term creditworthiness of both Brazil and Argentina, market experts said the ratings upgrades reflect the countries' strong fundamentals.
"It supports the view that is generally held that the fundamentals are solid," said Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at BankBoston Corp.
